nameStory: The Humped Ancula gets its name from the distinctive humps or bumps that rise from its back, giving it a lumpy, textured appearance. The genus name 'Ancula' comes from Latin, referring to a small servant or attendant, perhaps because these tiny sea slugs seem to quietly go about their business on the seafloor. It's also called the Atlantic Ancula since it's found throughout Atlantic coastal waters.
description: The Humped Ancula is a small, translucent sea slug that belongs to a group called nudibranchs (pronounced 'NEW-dih-branks'), which means 'naked gills.' These marine snails have lost their shells through evolution and instead sport soft, jelly-like bodies. They're typically small creatures, usually less than an inch long, with a whitish or pale body decorated with distinctive bumps or tubercles on their back. Like all nudibranchs, they breathe through feathery gills that stick out from their body.

idTips.label: Characteristic humps
idTips.description: Look for several rounded bumps or tubercles rising from the back - these feel soft and squishy to the touch, like tiny gel-filled pillows

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The body appears almost see-through with a whitish or pale coloration, sometimes with a slight pinkish or yellowish tint

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and elongated, typically less than an inch long, with a slug-like body that feels smooth and gelatinous

idTips.label: Tentacle-like projections
idTips.description: Two horn-like sensory tentacles (rhinophores) project from the head area, often appearing club-shaped at the tips

idTips.label: Gill arrangement
idTips.description: Feathery gills are arranged in a circular pattern around the rear of the body, retracting quickly when disturbed

habitat: Humped Anculas live in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores and tide pools. They're most commonly found crawling on hard surfaces like rocks, pier pilings, and kelp holdfasts in the lower intertidal and subtidal zones. Look for them in areas with good water circulation where their preferred food - tiny bryozoans (colonial animals that look like moss) - grows abundantly.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to warm, making this a good time to spot them moving across rocks during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and actively feeding. Best time for tide pool observations during extreme low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Can be found during autumn tide pooling expeditions.
seasonality.winter: Less visible as they retreat to deeper, more protected waters, though dedicated cold-water divers may still encounter them.

funFact: Humped Anculas are specialized hunters that feed almost exclusively on tiny colonial animals called bryozoans - and they can actually steal the stinging cells from their prey and incorporate them into their own skin for protection, essentially turning their victim's weapons into their own defense system!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, pale nudibranchs, but the distinctive humped tubercles on the back are your key identifying feature. Remember: 'Humps equal Humped Ancula' - no other common New England nudibranch has quite the same bumpy-backed appearance.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Latin, referring to how these sea slugs have their breathing organs exposed on the outside of their bodies rather than hidden inside a shell like most other snails. They're actually highly evolved marine snails that gave up the protection of shells in favor of other survival strategies.
compareHints: Since Humped Ancula is the only Ancula species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other small dorid nudibranchs in the region. Unlike smooth-backed species, the Humped Ancula's distinctive tubercles make it relatively easy to identify. Other dorids may have different textures like ridges or spines, but the soft, rounded humps are unique to this species.
